t.7.31.1: Then the greatly radiant Rāma, out of wonder, bowing low, once again addressed these words to Agastya, the best of sages.
t.7.31.2: O blessed one, O best of the twice-born, were the worlds empty then, that Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, met with no defeat anywhere in them?
t.7.31.3: Or were those rulers of the earth then lacking in valor, so that many kings were defeated and stripped of their excellent weapons?
t.7.31.4: Having heard the words of Rāghava, the blessed sage Agastya, laughing, spoke to Rāma as Pitāmaha might speak to Īśvara.
t.7.31.5: Thus, harassing the kings, O bull among kings, Rāvaṇa roamed over the earth, O Rāma, O lord of the earth.
t.7.31.6: Then he reached the city named Māhiṣmatī, splendid as the city of heaven, where Vasuretas was ever supremely present.
t.7.31.7: Its king, Arjuna by name, was equal in prowess to Vasuretas, and for him Agni always lay in a pit of reeds.
t.7.31.8: On that very day, the mighty Arjuna, lord of the Haihayas, that sovereign, had gone to the Narmadā with his women to sport.
t.7.31.9: But Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, asked his ministers: "Where is that king of yours, Arjuna, today? You should tell me quickly."
t.7.31.10: I, Rāvaṇa, have come here, eager for battle with the best of men. Let my arrival be announced to him by you without delay or agitation.
t.7.31.11: Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, those very wise ministers told the lord of the rākṣasas of the king's absence.
t.7.31.12: Having heard from the citizens that Arjuna had gone away, the son of Viśravas withdrew and came to the Vindhya, a mountain resembling the Himavat.
t.7.31.13: Rāvaṇa beheld the Vindhya, which seemed to have pierced the clouds and to have reared up out of the earth, as though it were scraping the sky.
t.7.31.14: It was crowned with a thousand peaks, its caves were the haunt of lions, and with the cool waters tumbling down its cascades it seemed to roar with laughter.
t.7.31.15: He beheld that great and lofty height, which had become a very heaven through the Devas, Dānavas and Gandharvas, together with hosts of Apsarases and Kiṃnaras, who sported there with their women.
t.7.31.17: Then Rāvaṇa, beholding the Vindhya mountain, full of meteors and caves and resembling the Himavat, went on to the Narmadā.
t.7.31.16: With its streaming rivers, like spread hoods with flickering tongues, it stood as though vomiting forth water beyond compare.
t.7.31.18: The sacred river, whose waters roll the stones along, flowing toward the western ocean, its pools churned up by buffaloes, sṛmaras, lions, tigers, bears and the finest elephants, scorched by the heat and thirsty.
t.7.31.19: She was thronged with cakravāka birds together with kāraṇḍa ducks, with haṃsas and water-fowl, and with sārasa cranes, ever intoxicated with passion and calling out loudly.
t.7.31.20: Her, whose ear-ornaments were fashioned from blossoming trees, whose breasts were a pair of cakravāka birds, whose hips were the broad sandbanks, and whose lovely girdle was a line of swans.
t.7.31.21: Her limbs were anointed with the pollen of flowers, her spotless garment was the foam of the waters, her touch was felt by those who plunged into her waters, and her lovely eyes were full-blown lotuses.
t.7.31.23: Seated together with his ministers on her lovely sandbank, adorned with many kinds of flowers, that bull among Rākṣasas, the lord of the Rākṣasas, felt the joy born of beholding the Narmadā.
t.7.31.24: Then Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, laughing playfully, spoke there to his ministers Mārīca, Śuka and Sāraṇa.
t.7.31.25: This sun, maker of fierce heat, which with its thousand rays has seemingly turned the world to gold, has reached the middle of the sky; yet, knowing that I am seated here, the maker of day behaves like the moon.
t.7.31.26: Cool from the waters of the Narmadā, fragrant and dispelling weariness, this wind, out of fear of me, blows here with great restraint.
t.7.31.27: And this Narmadā too, best of rivers and increaser of delight, stands like a frightened woman, her fish, birds and waves hidden and still.
t.7.31.22: Swiftly descending from the Puṣpaka, the Ten-faced one plunged into the Narmadā, best of rivers, as if into a beloved and excellent woman.
t.7.31.28: So you, wounded in battle by the weapons of kings equal to Indra, were drenched with blood as though with the juice of sandalwood.
t.7.31.29: So plunge, all of you, into the Narmadā, bestower of happiness upon men, just as mighty elephants in rut, led by Mahāpadma, plunge into the Gaṅgā.
t.7.31.30: Having bathed in this great river, you will be freed from your sin.
t.7.31.31: I too, here on this sandbank shining like the autumn moon, shall slowly make an offering of flowers to Umāpati.
t.7.31.32: Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, Mārīca, Śuka and Sāraṇa, together with Mahodara and Dhūmrākṣa, plunged into the Narmadā.
t.7.31.33: The river Narmadā was churned up by those elephant-like lords of the Rākṣasas, just as the Gaṅgā is stirred by the mighty elephants Vāmana, Añjana, Padma and the others.
t.7.31.34: Then those Rākṣasas, having bathed in the excellent waters of the Narmadā and come out, gathered flowers for Rāvaṇa's offering.
t.7.31.35: On the lovely sandbank of the Narmadā, whose radiance was like that of a bright white cloud, the lords of the Rākṣasas raised in a moment a mountain made of flowers.
t.7.31.36: As soon as the flowers had been brought, Rāvaṇa, lord of the Rākṣasas, went down into the river to bathe, like a mighty elephant descending into the Gaṅgā.
t.7.31.37: Having bathed there according to rule and having recited the most excellent prayer, that Rāvaṇa came up out of the waters of the Narmadā.
t.7.31.38: Seven rākṣasas followed Rāvaṇa as he went along with joined palms. Wherever Rāvaṇa, the lord of the rākṣasas, went, there a liṅga made of jāmbūnada gold was carried.
t.7.31.39: Rāvaṇa, having installed that liṅga in the middle of an altar of sand, worshipped it with perfumes and with flowers fragrant as nectar.
t.7.31.40: Then, having duly worshipped Hara, the supreme one, remover of the affliction of the good, bestower of boons, whose ornament is the rays of the moon, the night-roamer sang, and stretching out his long arms, he danced.
